Concept 01

Dataset & Components

A Component is a Rust struct stored as Arrow columns. A Dataset is every component together, sharing one row count.

In one line
The container that holds your data as columns, not rows
You need
Nothing beyond saci-core. No feature flag.
Read this if
You are about to define your first component, or you want to know why a Row index stops being valid

What a Dataset holds

Four things, and the central one is one Arrow RecordBatch per registered component, with every batch sharing the dataset's row count. That shared count is what makes a single Row index mean the same record in all of them. A component may hold fewer rows than the count, which a windowing processor's reduced result component does, and never more.

columnar data bookkeeping not columnar, not serialized

A Dataset is useful on its own for ad-hoc columnar work; a Pipeline wraps one together with a set of systems.

Defining a Component

A component names itself and provides an Arrow schema. Conversion to and from RecordBatch goes through serde_arrow, so deriving Serialize and Deserialize is enough for most types.

Rusta component is a struct plus a schema
use std::sync::Arc;
use arrow_schema::{DataType, Field, Schema};
use saci_core::prelude::*;
use serde::{Deserialize, Serialize};

#[derive(Serialize, Deserialize, Clone)]
struct Price {
    symbol: String,
    value: f64,
}

impl Component for Price {
    fn name() -> &'static str { "Price" }

    fn schema() -> Arc<Schema> {
        Arc::new(Schema::new(vec![
            Field::new("symbol", DataType::Utf8,    false),
            Field::new("value",  DataType::Float64, false),
        ]))
    }
}

Typed FieldRef constants are optional. Systems use them to declare access and ComponentView uses them to fetch typed columns, and neither costs more than a string compare.

Rustoptional, and worth it
impl Price {
    pub const SYMBOL: FieldRef<Price> = FieldRef::new("symbol");
    pub const VALUE:  FieldRef<Price> = FieldRef::new("value");
}

Registering and appending

Register every component before the first append. Registration reserves the component's batch slot, and appending afterwards would break the shared row count, so register_component returns an error once rows exist.

Rustregister, then append
let mut data = Dataset::new();
data.register_component::<Price>()?;

let rows = vec![
    Price { symbol: "AAPL".into(), value: 150.0 },
    Price { symbol: "MSFT".into(), value: 300.0 },
    Price { symbol: "GOOG".into(), value: 2_800.0 },
];

let range: std::ops::Range<Row> = data.append::<Price>(&rows)?;
assert_eq!(data.rows(), 3);
Constraint

Every component must receive the same number of new rows per append cycle. Appending 100 rows to one component and 50 to another leaves the dataset inconsistent, and later reads may panic.

Or set everything up in one chain with the builder:

Rustbuilder form
let data = Dataset::builder()
    .with::<Price>()
    .with::<Volume>()
    .with_resource(MarketCalendar::default())
    .build();

Reading columns

Three ways in, from most raw to most convenient:

Rustpick the level you need
// 1. Raw Arrow, for whole-batch operations
let batch: &RecordBatch = data.columns::<Price>().expect("registered");
let value: &ArrayRef    = data.column::<Price>("value").expect("field");

// 2. Typed view: borrows the batch, hands back concrete Arrow arrays
let prices = data.view::<Price>()?;
let value  = prices.f64(Price::VALUE)?;
let symbol = prices.str(Price::SYMBOL)?;
for i in 0..prices.len() {
    println!("{} = {}", symbol.value(i), value.value(i));
}

// 3. Back into Rust structs. Allocates, so keep it for small batches.
let restored: Vec<Price> = Price::from_record_batch(batch)?;

ComponentView accessors are named after the Arrow type: f64, i64, u64, bool, str and ts_ns. They return concrete array types like &Float64Array, so you index without downcasting.

Soft delete and compaction

Deleting a row flips one bit. The bytes stay put until you compact, and compaction renumbers every row.

Rustdelete, then reclaim
data.mark_dead(Row::new(0));
assert!(!data.is_alive(Row::new(0)));
assert_eq!(data.live_rows(), data.rows() - 1);

if data.should_compact() {
    data.compact()?;  // invalidates existing Row indices
}

Resources

A resource is a plain Rust singleton stored beside the columns, keyed by TypeId. Use one for configuration, a lookup table, or summary output: anything that is not per-row.

Rustnot columnar
struct FxRates { eur: f64, gbp: f64 }

data.insert_resource(FxRates { eur: 1.08, gbp: 1.27 });

let rates = data.get_resource::<FxRates>().expect("inserted");
assert_eq!(rates.eur, 1.08);

// Mutation needs &mut Dataset
data.get_resource_mut::<FxRates>().unwrap().gbp = 1.30;

Systems declare resource access the same way they declare fields:

Rustdeclared access
SystemMeta::new("convert")
    .read_resource::<FxRates>()    // shared read
    .write_resource::<Report>();   // exclusive write

Resource conflicts are tracked per TypeId, not per field. Two systems writing the same resource type always land in different stages.

Arrow IPC round-trip

A dataset serializes to Arrow IPC. Those are the same bytes the distributed runner uses for checkpoints and the same bytes that cross the WebAssembly boundary. The wire format reference pins their layout. Encoding sizes the output buffer from the batch's own memory footprint up front, which avoids repeated regrowth as it writes.

Rustencode and decode
// Encode
let mut buf = Vec::new();
data.write_ipc(&mut buf)?;

// Decode. read_ipc takes any std::io::Read.
let restored = Dataset::read_ipc(&mut &buf[..])?;
assert_eq!(restored.rows(), data.rows());
What IPC leaves out, and what it checks

Resources are absent from the payload, so re-attach them after decoding. Every component in the stream must hold at most the row count the alive bitmap declares, or read_ipc rejects the stream as corrupt. Fewer rows is legal. That is a windowing processor's reduced result component.

The Row type

Row is a transparent u32 index into the columnar storage. append hands back the Range<Row> it just wrote, which is the safest way to act on rows you own.

Rustoperate on what you appended
let range = data.append::<Price>(&rows)?;
for row in range.clone() {
    if should_drop(row) {
        data.mark_dead(row);
    }
}
